PCB Design & Signal Integrity
PCB Thermal Relief Pad Design: Spoke Count, Width, Air Gap and Current per Spoke

A thermal relief pad joins a pin to a copper plane through a few narrow spokes, so the joint can reach solder temperature. With well sized spokes, the pad solders cleanly and still carries its current.

Spoke width Air gap Spoke count IPC 2221 Current calculator

Thermal relief spokes decide how easily a pad solders and how much current it can carry into the plane. Below you will find the usual numbers, the formula, a calculator and field fixes.

Hello everyone, today we are going to learn pcb thermal relief pad design, from spoke width and air gap to the current each spoke can safely carry.
Quick Answer

What is PCB thermal relief and why is it used?

PCB thermal relief is a pad connection where a few narrow copper spokes, separated by an air gap, join a pin to a copper pour or plane instead of solid copper. The spokes slow the heat that would flow into the plane, so the joint reaches solder temperature. For example, four 0.3 mm spokes in 1 oz outer copper carry about 1.00 A each, or 4.00 A in total, at a 10 °C rise.

What Is PCB Thermal Relief?

A pcb thermal relief is a pad connection where a ring of air gap surrounds the pad and only two to four narrow copper spokes bridge it to the surrounding plane. It exists so that soldering heat stays in the joint long enough to melt the solder, while the spokes still give an electrical connection to the net.

Key Facts
  • Typical relief: 4 spokes at 90 degrees, often rotated 45 degrees on dense boards.
  • Common starting values: about 0.25 to 0.4 mm spoke width and 0.2 to 0.3 mm air gap.
  • Altium suggests 8 mil spokes with 10 mil clearance for most parts.
  • IPC 2221 covers it in section 9.1.3, Thermal Relief in Conductor Planes.
  • Spoke current follows the IPC 2221 trace formula.

You meet this on almost every board with a ground or power pour. If you are new to pours, read our copper pour guidelines first, because the relief settings live inside the pour or plane rules of your CAD tool.

Do You Know?

A solid plane connection acts as a heat sink during soldering, which is why ground pins tied straight into a heavy inner plane are so hard to rework with a hand iron.

Advertisement

What Is the Purpose of Thermal Relief on a PCB?

The relief lets a pad solder easily while keeping a good electrical connection to the plane. Copper conducts heat very well, so a pad merged into a large pour keeps losing heat to that pour during soldering.

If the pad never reaches the solder liquidus temperature, you get a cold joint, poor hole fill in wave soldering, or a long dwell that cooks nearby parts. On small SMD passives the same imbalance makes one end melt before the other, and the part can lift up and tombstone during reflow.

In the diagram, heat can only leave through the four spokes, and their small cross section gives the pad time to reach solder temperature. For heat that you actually want to move into the plane, a different tool applies, which we cover in thermal vias for heat dissipation.

Direct connect

The pad merges into the pour with no gap, so it has the lowest resistance but is hardest to solder.

Best for: High current pins, thermal vias, reflow only power pads
Solid
4 spoke relief

The default in most CAD tools, with spokes at 90 degrees or rotated 45 degrees.

Best for: General through hole and SMD pads on pours
Default
2 spoke relief

Only two spokes, usually opposite each other, for an even lower heat path.

Best for: Small 0402 and 0201 passives prone to tombstoning
Light
Inner plane thermal

On negative inner planes the relief is a flashed shape set by inner and outer diameter and spoke width.

Best for: Through hole pins on buried ground or power planes
Plane

PCB Thermal Relief Spoke Width, Air Gap and Count

For most boards, start with four spokes about 0.25 to 0.4 mm wide and an air gap of about 0.2 to 0.3 mm, then adjust for current and copper weight. These are common fabricator and CAD defaults, and Altium gives 8 mil spokes with 10 mil clearance as a value that works for most components.

ParameterTypical start valueWhat changes it
Spoke count4 (2 for tiny passives)Current, solder method, space around pad
Spoke width0.25 to 0.4 mm (10 to 16 mil)Current per spoke, fab minimum trace
Air gap0.2 to 0.3 mm (8 to 12 mil)Fab minimum clearance, copper weight
Copper weight1 oz outer, 0.5 to 1 oz innerHeavier copper needs a larger gap

Keep every spoke wider than the fabricator minimum trace width and every gap wider than its minimum spacing, which you will find in our essential PCB design rules. On high voltage nets the air gap is also a clearance, so check it against creepage and clearance values before you shrink it.

Quick Tip

Set the relief once as a rule on the pour or plane, not pad by pad, and add a higher priority rule for power nets.

How Do You Calculate PCB Thermal Relief Current per Spoke?

Treat each spoke as a short trace and apply the IPC 2221 current formula, then multiply by the number of spokes that really connect. The formula is I = k × ΔT^0.44 × A^0.725, with k = 0.048 for outer layers and 0.024 for inner layers, ΔT in °C and A in square mils.

Solved example: 4 spokes, 0.3 mm wide, 1 oz outer copper, 10 °C rise
Width = 0.3 ÷ 0.0254 = 11.81 mil
Thickness of 1 oz = 1.378 mil
A = 11.81 × 1.378 = 16.28 mil²
I = 0.048 × 10^0.44 × 16.28^0.725
I = 0.048 × 2.754 × 7.56 = 1.00 A per spoke
Total = 4 × 1.00 = 4.00 A

The same spoke on an inner layer, with k = 0.024, carries only half as much, about 0.50 A per spoke or 2.00 A in total. So a relief that is fine on the top layer can be the weak link in a buried power plane.

Current does not rise in proportion to width, because area is raised to the power 0.725. Doubling width from 0.25 mm to 0.5 mm lifts current only from 0.87 A to 1.45 A per spoke.

Per spoke 1.00 A, total 4.00 A for 4 spokes

Treat the result as conservative, since IPC 2221 was built for long traces and a short spoke also sheds heat into the pad and plane. For a full trace check, the PCB trace width calculator uses the same equation, and this trace width tool is handy for quick cross checks.

When Should You Not Use Thermal Relief?

Skip the relief when the pad must carry high current or move heat, and the board is reflow soldered so plane heating is less of a problem. Thermal vias under an exposed pad, high current connector pins and stitching vias are the usual cases for direct connect.

Thermal relief
  • Easier hand soldering and rework
  • Better hole fill in wave soldering
  • Less tombstoning on small passives
Direct connect
  • Lowest resistance and inductance to the plane
  • Best heat path from part to copper
  • Harder to solder, needs more preheat

Spoke inductance matters on decoupling and fast return paths. For those pads see our notes on how decoupling capacitors work and on the PCB return current path.

Do Vias Need Thermal Relief?

Most vias do not need thermal relief, because nobody solders into a via and reflow heats the whole board evenly. Signal vias, stitching vias and thermal vias are normally set to direct connect.

The exception is a via that doubles as a test point or a hand soldered wire point, which behaves like a through hole pad. The current limit of the via barrel itself is covered in PCB via current capacity, and the via styles in through hole, blind and buried vias.

IPC 2221A Generic Standard on Printed Board Design

How to Set Up PCB Thermal Relief Step by Step

Define the relief in your pour and plane rules, add exceptions for power and via nets, then confirm with a design rule check. The steps are the same in KiCad, Altium, OrCAD and Eagle.

1
List the pads
Note the net, current and solder method of every pad on a pour or plane.
2
Set default relief
Use 4 spokes, about 0.3 mm wide, with a 0.25 mm gap in the pour or plane rule.
3
Check current
Run the calculator for power pins and widen or add spokes if needed.
4
Add exceptions
Set direct connect for thermal and stitching vias, and 2 spokes for tiny passives.
5
Run DRC
Clear any starved thermal warnings caused by blocked spokes.
6
Review Gerbers
Confirm every inner plane relief is a full ring with spokes.

Check inner layers carefully, because on a negative plane a wrong flash is easy to miss. Our guides on ground plane design and layer stackup design explain how those planes are built.

Troubleshooting PCB Thermal Relief Problems

Most pcb thermal relief problems show up at assembly or at first power up, and each symptom points to one setting.

SymptomLikely causeFix
Cold or grainy joint on ground pinDirect connect to large planeAdd 4 spoke relief or more preheat
Poor hole fill in wave solderToo many or too wide spokesNarrow spokes, check plane copper weight
Tombstoned 0402 capacitorOne pad on pour, other on thin traceUse 2 spokes so both pads heat evenly
Spoke burnt or pad warm in useSpoke current too low for the loadWiden spokes, add spokes or direct connect
DRC starved thermal warningTrace or via blocks a spokeMove the copper or rotate spokes 45 degrees
Myth: Thermal relief is only needed for through hole parts.
Fact: Small SMD passives on pours also benefit, because uneven pad heating causes tombstoning in reflow.
Myth: More spokes always make a better joint.
Fact: More spokes improve current and heat flow out of the pad, so the pad gets harder to solder.
Myth: The relief reduces current capacity only a little.
Fact: Four 0.3 mm spokes on an inner layer carry about 2 A by IPC 2221, which can be far below the pin rating.
Do You Know?

Spoke resistance is small but not zero. Using the method in our trace resistance calculation, a 0.5 mm long, 0.3 mm wide spoke in 1 oz copper works out near 1 milliohm, so four in parallel add only a fraction of a milliohm.

Video: When to Apply Thermal Relief Pads

This short Altium Academy video shows when a pad should get pcb thermal relief and when direct connect is the better choice.

PCB Thermal Relief Review Checklist

Before you send files to the fabricator, run through this pcb thermal relief list once for every board with pours or planes.

  • Every pad on a pour or plane has the intended connect style
  • Spoke width is above the fab minimum trace width
  • Air gap is above the fab minimum spacing and the voltage clearance
  • Power pins pass the spoke current calculation with margin
  • Thermal and stitching vias are set to direct connect
  • No starved thermal warnings remain in DRC
  • Inner plane reliefs checked in a Gerber viewer
Quick Tip

For heavy copper boards of 2 oz and above, widen the air gap a little, since thick copper etches with more undercut and narrow gaps can bridge.

PCB Thermal Relief FAQ

What is the difference between thermal relief and direct connect on a PCB?

Thermal relief joins a pad to the plane through narrow spokes across an air gap, while direct connect merges the pad into solid copper. Relief makes soldering easier.

Direct connect gives lower resistance and a better heat path. It suits thermal vias and high current pins on reflow soldered boards.

How many spokes should a pcb thermal relief pad have for normal parts?

Four spokes is the usual default for through hole and SMD pads on a pour. Two spokes can help on 0402 and 0201 passives that tend to tombstone.

Use more or wider spokes when a power pin needs extra current. Always confirm that every spoke actually connects in the DRC.

How do you calculate the current a thermal relief spoke can carry?

Use the IPC 2221 formula I = k × ΔT^0.44 × A^0.725 with k = 0.048 for outer layers. A 0.3 mm spoke in 1 oz copper at 10 °C rise gives about 1 amp.

Multiply by the number of connected spokes for the total. Four spokes give about 4 amps in this example.

What spoke width and air gap should I use for thermal relief?

A common start is a spoke width of 0.25 to 0.4 mm and an air gap of 0.2 to 0.3 mm. Altium suggests 8 mil spokes with 10 mil clearance for most parts.

Stay above the fabricator minimum trace and spacing. Widen the gap on heavy copper boards.

What causes a starved thermal error in a PCB design rule check?

A starved thermal means some spokes could not connect because a trace, via or clearance blocked them. The pad then has fewer spokes than the rule asks for.

Move the blocking copper or rotate the spokes to 45 degrees. Then run the check again until every relief has its full count.

Should thermal vias under a power IC use thermal relief or direct connect?

Thermal vias should use direct connect, because their only job is to move heat into the plane. Spokes would choke that heat path and defeat the purpose.

Reflow heats the whole board, so soldering the exposed pad is still fine. Follow the IC datasheet for via count and pitch.

What We Learn Today

  • A pcb thermal relief joins a pad to a plane through two to four narrow spokes across an air gap so the joint solders properly.
  • Start with four spokes about 0.3 mm wide and a 0.25 mm gap, then check fabricator minimums, voltage clearance and copper weight.
  • Estimate spoke current with the IPC 2221 formula, where four 0.3 mm spokes in 1 oz outer copper carry about 4 amps.
